analysis.one_liner: Lets anyone put up to $18,000 per couple a year into tax-free health savings accounts, usable for premiums.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would sharply expand health savings accounts (HSAs), special accounts where money set aside for medical bills is not taxed. It would raise the annual contribution cap to $9,000 per person or $18,000 per married couple, let anyone open an HSA without also having a high-deductible insurance plan, allow HSA money to pay insurance premiums and direct primary care memberships, and cut the penalty for spending HSA money on non-medical things from 20% to 10%. It was referred to the tax-writing committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with spare cash to park in a tax-sheltered account. HSAs are tax-free going in, grow tax-free, and come out tax-free for medical costs, so the biggest deduction goes to people in high tax brackets who can afford to contribute the full $9,000-$18,000 a year. Dropping the high-deductible-plan requirement also means any saver, not just people with that coverage, could open an account.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Higher-income households who can max out accounts

how_it_helps.text: Raises the annual HSA contribution cap to $9,000 for individuals and $18,000 for joint filers, indexed to inflation
Eliminates the requirement that an HSA holder be enrolled in a high-deductible health plan, so any taxpayer could open an account
Allows HSA funds to pay health insurance premiums and direct primary care service arrangements, and repeals the restriction on over-the-counter medications
Reduces the extra tax on HSA withdrawals not used for medical expenses from 20% to 10%

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. Every dollar contributed is a dollar not taxed, and larger caps plus a wider pool of eligible account holders means more federal revenue foregone; the bill contains no offset to pay for it. Treasury analysts have long found that HSA tax benefits flow disproportionately to higher-income filers.

drawbacks.text: The deduction is worth the most to people in high tax brackets who can afford to contribute thousands of dollars a year they do not need for current bills; households living paycheck to paycheck get little or nothing from it
Allowing anyone to open an HSA and letting HSA funds pay premiums could draw healthier people out of comprehensive insurance arrangements, leaving plans covering sicker, more expensive patients
The bill text contains no revenue offset, so the cost of the expanded tax break would add to deficits

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does give account holders real flexibility, and some middle-class families with high medical bills would value larger contribution room. But an HSA only pays off if you have thousands of spare dollars a year and a tax bill worth sheltering, so the benefit is concentrated among households that already have savings, while the cost, foregone federal revenue, is spread across everyone. It is a tax cut aimed up the income scale dressed as a health bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on January 4, 2017, the same day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dave Brat introduced the bill on January 4, 2017, the first week of the 115th Congress, joined by 18 Republican cosponsors
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the panel with jurisdiction over the tax code, on the day of introduction
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point in the two-year Congress

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No industry lost anything because the bill never moved, and general taxpayers are spared the cost of a larger tax shelter skewed toward higher-income households. People who wanted broader HSA flexibility, who were disproportionately higher earners, got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers spared an upward-skewed tax break

for.name: Rep. Dave Brat
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House on January 4, 2017

for.name: 18 of 241 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for all tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 18 cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill never progressed far enough to attract Democratic support or a floor vote.

industries.industry: Banks and financial firms that administer HSAs
industries.note: Bigger contribution caps and an end to the high-deductible-plan requirement would create more accounts and larger balances for banks and account administrators to hold and charge fees on. Some savers would gain flexibility too, but the expansion is funded by foregone tax revenue.

industries.industry: Health insurers, especially high-deductible plan sellers
industries.note: Letting HSA money pay premiums opens a new payment channel for insurers, but decoupling HSAs from high-deductible plans removes the coupling that has steered customers into those products. The effect on insurers' bottom lines is genuinely two-sided.

The $18,000 couple cap and the removal of plan requirements make HSAs a more powerful tax shelter for people with money to save; the revenue cost falls on taxpayers broadly, who are on the other side of the ledger.
The bill explicitly makes direct primary care memberships a qualified use of HSA funds, opening a paying customer base for subscription-based medical practices.
